soil-water-288.title: SWAT, a free model of whole watersheds
soil-water-288.text: Universities and government agencies around the world reach for the same free program when they model a landscape's water. The Soil and Water Assessment Tool, known as SWAT, is an open-source hydrology model and map-based simulation sponsored by the USDA. SWAT is a geographic version of {{ref:soil-water-107}}, and it works alongside commercial mapping software such as ArcGIS.

soil-water-281.title: Mineral dust, the soil that travels by sky
soil-water-281.text: Every year the world's winds lift somewhere between 1000 and 5000 million tons of soil into the air. That cloud is mineral dust, an atmospheric aerosol of suspended soil minerals. It is mostly crustal oxides such as SiO2, Al2O3, FeO, Fe2O3 and CaO, plus the carbonates CaCO3 and MgCO3. Most comes from deserts, but about a quarter may come from land-use change and human-made {{ref:soil-env-072}}. The Sahara is the largest source, at 60 to 200 million tons a year. Its dust feeds the Amazon rainforest and to phytoplankton in the Mediterranean. Spring dust from the Gobi, called Asian dust, harms visibility and health, yet is thought to enrich soils with trace minerals. Farming pressure and spreading desert worsened it after 1950. Soil moisture, vegetation cover, wind speed and soil type control emissions. North American dustfall rose 60% in the 1800s as land disturbance accelerated. Drought is harder to pin down: modern observations link it to more dust, but lake-sediment records of ancient megadroughts disagree.

soil-water-291.title: RUSLE, the soil loss equation revised
soil-water-291.text: An equation first built for farm fields is still among North America's busiest erosion tools. The Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation, or RUSLE, is an updated form of {{ref:soil-water-041}}. With the WEPP model, it is one of the two most widely used erosion models on the continent. Various techniques now compute its five factors. The support practice factor, P, is often estimated from land use and slope gradient, and a lower value means better erosion control. Much research on eroding mined land focuses on fitting or improving its parameters.

soil-water-287.title: Predicting how much a field loses to wind
soil-water-287.text: Wind moves soil in bursts. Grains sit still until the wind passes a critical speed. Then the erosion rate climbs with the cube of the friction velocity, a measure of the wind's drag on the ground. The wind erosion equation estimates a field's potential average annual soil loss to wind as E = f(I, K, C, L, V). The five inputs are soil erodibility, ridge roughness, a climatic factor, the unsheltered distance across the field and the equivalent vegetative cover. Friction velocity is calculated from measured wind speed using the von Kármán constant, about 0.4. Most wind records come from airports and military bases, often only since the Second World War.

soil-water-274.title: Where moving sediment finally comes to rest
soil-water-274.text: Everything that erosion carries away must eventually land somewhere. Deposition is the geological process by which sediment, soil and rock are added to a landform or landmass. Wind, ice, water and gravity all carry weathered material, and they drop it in layers when the flow loses enough kinetic energy. The tipping point has a name, the null point hypothesis: deposition begins when the forces moving sediment can no longer overcome gravity and friction. Grain size shapes how this plays out. Large grains come to rest when the water's drag on the bed and its turbulence fall too low. Grains held up in the water may still drift some way as they sink. Fine silt and clay particles settle one by one, following {{ref:soil-phys-188}}. In seawater, though, they flocculate, bonding electrically into clumps called flocs that sink together. Deposition is not only about broken rock. It can build sediment from organic or chemical matter too. Chalk forms from the skeletons of plankton, and coal from plant material laid down without oxygen.

soil-water-272.title: Denudation, the slow lowering of the land
soil-water-272.text: Mountains are pushed up faster than they wear down. Average mountain-building can run eight times faster than the maximum average denudation. Denudation is the sum of the processes by which moving water, ice, wind and waves wear down Earth's surface and lower its elevation and relief. Denudation is broader than {{ref:soil-water-002}}. Erosion moves soil and rock from place to place, while denudation adds up everything that lowers the surface. It combines mechanical, biological and chemical {{ref:soil-found-052}}, erosion and {{ref:soil-water-053}}, and it carries away both solid particles and dissolved material. Its pace depends on human activity, living organisms, climate, rock type, topography and tectonic activity. Tectonics works on both sides of the ledger. Uplift, volcanoes and earthquakes expose fresh crust to weathering and erosion. As denudation strips weight from the crust, the crust can rise further. The idea has a long history. It goes back to 1785 and to Hutton and Playfair, who argued that landscapes are worn down to near sea level. That view inspired planation theories such as William Morris Davis's peneplanation cycle, which faded after 1964.

soil-water-275.title: Sedimentation: when falling grains finally stop
soil-water-275.text: Settling is the fall of particles through a liquid; sedimentation is where that fall ends, with the particles at rest against a barrier. How they fall depends on the particle. Sand grains, called type 1, settle singly at constant velocity. Type 2 particles flocculate, so their settling speed changes as they clump. Above 1000 mg/L, type 3 particles settle together as a zone. Deep-sea sediment builds up at under 3 millimetres per thousand years; parts of major deltas gain several metres. Restoring the exchange of water and sediment between rivers and delta plains helps sinking deltas keep their height.

soil-water-284.title: Siltation, when eroded soil chokes the water
soil-water-284.text: A layer of mud just 1 mm thick can kill coral polyps. That sensitivity makes siltation one of erosion's costliest side effects. Siltation is water pollution by fine {{ref:soil-phys-013}} and clay particles, both as extra sediment suspended in the water and as unwanted fine deposits on the bottom. It usually starts with {{ref:soil-water-001}}, or with sediment spilled during dredging and dumping. In the countryside the source is typically soil degraded by intensive or poor farming, especially fine-grained soils such as {{ref:soil-form-106}}. In towns it is construction sites stripped of vegetation. Erosion at the source may amount to a fraction of a millimetre a year, too little to measure there. So sediment is measured in transport instead, as concentration times discharge: 50 mg/L flowing at 30 m3/s carries 1.5 kg/s. Suspended sediment disrupts filter-feeding animals, and deposits bury them. Hard-bottom communities and mussel and oyster banks suffer more than sand and mud bottoms. The first defense is keeping land covered so it does not erode. The second is trapping sediment before it reaches streams, and construction sites use short exposure times and silt screens. Silt also fills shipping channels and channels that carry water to crops, where dredging is often the only cure once it settles.

soil-water-277.title: How rivers carve, carry and build with sediment
soil-water-277.text: Each year the Yellow River is estimated to deliver 796 million tons of sediment to the sea. The Mississippi carries 406 million tons and the Po 67 million. Fluvial sediment processes are the movement of sediment by rivers and streams, with the erosion, deposition and landforms they create. Flowing water drags on its bed and lowers it where the bed is weak or loose. The sediment it carries scrapes the bed, while the fragments themselves grind smaller and rounder, a wearing called attrition. Sediment travels in three ways: rolling along the bed as bed load, held up in the flow as {{ref:soil-water-286}}, or dissolved. A single ratio, the Rouse number, sorts the grains. It compares a grain's settling velocity with the water's upward velocity. Above 2.5 a grain moves as bed load, between 0.8 and 2.5 held up in the flow, and below 0.8 as wash load, the finest fraction. Water moves bigger grains than air does because it is denser and more viscous, and floods can roll cobbles and boulders. Where flow is fast, the river picks up more than it drops. Where it is slow, dropped particles build {{ref:soil-water-264}} of {{ref:soil-form-112}}. The moving bed shapes ripples, dunes and antidunes, which preserved in rock record the direction and strength of ancient flows.

soil-water-286.title: Suspended load: sediment carried by turbulence
soil-water-286.text: Muddy river water owes its color to grains that never touch the bottom. Suspended load is the part of a flow's sediment lifted off the bed and held up by turbulence. It is mostly fine sand, silt and clay, though strong flows carry coarser sand low in the water. It forms the middle layer of transport, between bed load below and the finest wash load above, described in {{ref:soil-water-249}}. Grains are fully suspended at Rouse numbers of 0.8 to 1.2 and half suspended at 1.2 to 2.5. When the flow slows, the load drops out.

soil-water-285.title: Stream power, the energy a river spends
soil-water-285.text: A river is a machine that spends energy on its own bed and banks. In the 1960s R. A. Bagnold put a number on that energy, now called stream power. It is the product of water density, gravitational acceleration, discharge and slope, Ω = ρgQS, in watts per unit length of channel. Dividing by channel width gives unit stream power. That lets rivers of different widths be compared and better estimates how much sediment a river can carry. Critical unit stream power is the power needed to move a grain of a given size, and it sets a river's competence, the largest grain it can shift. Several studies found a threshold at 30 to 35 W m−2, where rivers switch from stable to actively reshaping themselves. Engineers use stream power to design bridges and culverts that will not start erosion, and modelers use it to simulate how rivers cut down and landscapes evolve.

soil-water-270.title: Bank erosion: how rivers eat their sides
soil-water-270.text: Rivers wear away their banks as well as their beds, and bank erosion works in two linked steps. Flowing water removes particles directly, an action called fluvial erosion. Undercutting then sets up mass failure, when a bank's weight exceeds the soil's strength and it gives way. Groundwater seeping out of a bank can also erode it, a process called piping when concentrated. Roots usually slow bank erosion, though heavy trees can overload the bank top. Erosion pins, repeated surveys and aerial or satellite images track the rates.

soil-water-278.title: Headward erosion, a stream cutting uphill
soil-water-278.text: Some streams grow backward. Headward erosion cuts away the head of a channel, moving its origin upslope and lengthening the stream, valley or gully. Water gathering in channels gains speed and erosive power, and the steep gradient at the head speeds the cutting further. Given time, a stream can break into a neighboring watershed and capture its drainage, as the Shenandoah River did to Potomac tributaries. The rock decides the pattern: branching on uniform bedrock, trellis-like on alternating weak and strong rock, and rectangular on jointed rock.

soil-water-268.title: Aggradation, when rivers raise the land
soil-water-268.text: Give a river more sediment than it can carry and it starts building the ground up. Aggradation, also called alluviation, is that rise in land elevation as sediment is deposited. The Exner equation describes the balance between sediment in transport and sediment in the bed. Lowland rivers, deltas and {{ref:soil-water-293}} are typical settings, and their slow sinking often offsets the rise. A drier climate can trigger it: sparse plants bind less soil, so more sediment enters rivers just as their flow drops. A 2009 report found reduced aggradation raising flood risk in many deltas.

soil-water-276.title: Entrainment, the moment a grain lifts off
soil-water-276.text: Every grain on a riverbed waits for a certain speed. Entrainment is the incorporation of surface sediment into a moving fluid such as air, water or ice, and it starts erosion. Each grain size has its own entrainment velocity, the flow speed at which those grains begin to move. Once moving, grains keep traveling even below that speed, because friction with the bed drops. They settle only when the flow slows further, as {{ref:soil-water-250}} shows.

soil-water-282.title: Shear velocity, drag measured as speed
soil-water-282.text: Engineers often express the drag of a flow on its boundary as a speed. Shear velocity, also called friction velocity, is shear stress rewritten in units of velocity. It describes how particles and contaminants spread, how flow speed changes near a boundary, and how channels move sediment. It scales well with bedload transport, and in most rivers it is 5% to 10% of the mean flow velocity. Over land, the log wind profile gives it from wind speeds at two heights. Among trees or buildings, wind falls to zero at about 2/3 to 3/4 of obstacle height.
